items.title: Ministers to create new stalking offence and scrap need for proof of fear or distress
items.desc: Victims’ commissioner welcomes strengthening of law in England and Wales but calls for measures to tackle convicted stalkers Ministers will create a new stalking offence so that victims will no longer have to prove fear or distress to seek protection under the law, the Home Office has announced. Under current laws, the underlying offence of harassment in England and Wales, as well as additional factors such as the victim’s alarm, must be established for it to be considered stalking. The new law, alongside other changes, will focus on the perpetrator’s behaviour instead, officials said. Continue reading...

Three-quarters (76%) of those who took part in the UK-wide poll agreed social media had increased anxiety around parenting, while three out of five (59%) complained of “impossible expectations” and “feeling judged”. items.title: Cop31 collapse must be a catalyst for genuine climate action | Letters
items.desc: Readers on the failure of the climate talks in Turkey and the lessons we can learn The failure of Cop31, as commented on by Bill McGuire ( A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?, 24 November ), is the expression of the overwhelming momentum of the value system of a global culture that is wedded to the seemingly unstoppable expansion of our material production and consumption. The disjunction between peril and necessary action is explained by the impossibility of taming appetites that are insatiable. It is convenient to blame fossil fuel producers, and while they are obviously guilty parties, the ultimate problem is the continuing demand for their products. Continue reading...

items.title: Brussels on split-screen: where it flexes – and where it bends

items.title: Energy bills jump: how to switch providers and is it worth it?
items.desc: It is possible to switch to a better tariff and save money despite the 26% price rise in January Average energy bill in Great Britain predicted to rise to £2,166 The energy price cap in Great Britain will go up by 26% in January to the equivalent of £2,166 a year. However, your bills might not have to rise by the same amount. If you are paying a tariff that matches the price cap you could save by switching to something lower. And if you do it now, you could make a substantial saving. On Wednesday, the cheapest fixed tariff on the market, an 18-month fix from Fuse Energy, was priced at £1,754 for an average home – £412 below the new January cap. It’s worth noting that it’s the price of the energy you use that is fixed, not your bill – so you will still be charged according to what you use. Continue reading...

items.title: ‘Nature’s Ozempic’: oat sales soar as shoppers seek out foods that mimic effect of GLP-1s
items.desc: Porridge emerges as trend’s poster child with consumers looking to foods that help them feel full for longer, says Waitrose Sales of filling foods such as porridge oats that mimic the effect of taking weight-loss medication are booming on the back of social media hype billing them as “nature’s Ozempic” or “oatzempic”. Sales of Waitrose Scottish Oats are up 124% this year, according to the retailer’s annual food and drink report, which dissects the biggest trends sweeping the grocery aisles. A poll conducted for the report revealed that 64% of shoppers are “actively choosing to eat foods like oats that keep us feeling fuller for longer”. Continue reading...
